entries.title: A Friendly Yes Can Have a Limit

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: My friends invited me to watch a series. I'd like to go, but I don't want to spend the whole afternoon there.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Give a smaller yes: I'm up for one episode, then I'm heading out. Up for means interested or willing.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: I'm up for one episode, then I'm heading out. That sounds friendly, and it tells them what I'm agreeing to.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Exactly. A clear limit doesn't cancel the yes. It helps your friends understand it.

entries.prompt: Does she agree to one episode or the whole afternoon?
entries.answer: One episode. She accepts the invitation and names her limit.

entries.title: Available Does Not Always Mean Included

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: A fictional workshop advert says materials are available. You want to know whether you must pay extra. Which question helps? First: So everything must be free, right?

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Second: Are the materials included in the price, or available separately? Available tells you that you can get them. It doesn't tell you whether the advertised price covers them. Ask about the specific item before booking.

entries.prompt: Which question checks the price clearly: the first or the second?
entries.answer: The second. Ask whether the materials are included or available separately.

entries.title: Leave Warmly Without Inventing an Excuse
entries.hook: Enjoy it. Still leave on time.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Riley enjoyed an episode with her friends. Before arriving, she said she could stay until six. Now another episode is starting. She doesn't invent an urgent appointment or pretend she disliked the visit.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: She picks up her coat and says warmly: Thanks for having me. I'll leave you to it. Her friends can continue watching, and she can keep her plan.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: I'll leave you to it means I'm going, and you can carry on. A friendly tone keeps it from sounding annoyed.

entries.prompt: Is Riley asking her friends to stop, or letting them continue?
entries.answer: Letting them continue. She thanks them and leaves without an invented excuse.

entries.title: Check the Offer Without Sounding Accusing
entries.hook: Check the detail, not the person's honesty.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: The workshop says everything is included. But I can't see whether that includes taking my finished piece home. Should I say: You're hiding an extra charge?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: That assumes a motive you haven't checked. Try: Just so I'm clear, does the price include taking the finished piece home?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Just so I'm clear, does the price include taking the finished piece home? Now I'm asking about the actual detail, not accusing the organiser.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Right. In this fictional example, we still need their answer. A clear question checks the offer; it doesn't invent the result.

entries.prompt: Which opening checks your understanding: you're hiding something, or just so I'm clear?
entries.answer: Just so I'm clear. Then name the exact detail you want confirmed.
